questions.solution:
The Pythagorean identity: $\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = \mathbf{1}$, for every $\theta$.

Dividing through by $\cos^{2}\theta$ gives $\tan^{2}\theta + 1 = \sec^{2}\theta$, and by $\sin^{2}\theta$ gives $1 + \cot^{2}\theta = \operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta$.

$\cos 30° = \mathbf{\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}}$.

These come from two triangles: half an equilateral triangle gives the $30$–$60$ values, and a right-angled isosceles triangle gives the $45$ ones.

$y = \sin kx$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$, so here it is $\mathbf{\pi}$.

The wave is squashed horizontally by a factor of 2, fitting two complete cycles into the usual $2\pi$.

questions.q: How many solutions does $\sin\theta = 0.5$ have for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$?
questions.solution:
**Two** — at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

A calculator gives only the first. The sine is positive in the first **and second** quadrants, and missing the second solution is the standard error in this topic.

$\sin 2\theta = \mathbf{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}$.

$\cos 2\theta$ has three equivalent forms: $\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta$, $2\cos^{2}\theta - 1$ and $1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta$ — choose whichever leaves you with the function you want.
$\tan 45° = \mathbf{1}$ — the right-angled isosceles triangle has equal opposite and adjacent sides.

$\cos^{2}\theta = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64$, so $\cos\theta = \mathbf{0.8}$ (positive, since $\theta$ is acute).

The familiar $3$–$4$–$5$ triangle again.

questions.q: Find the maximum value of $3\sin x + 2$.
questions.solution: $\sin x$ reaches $1$, so the maximum is $3(1) + 2 = \mathbf{5}$ (and the minimum is $-1$).

questions.q: Solve $\cos\theta = 0$ for $0 \le \theta \le \pi$, giving the answer as $\dfrac{k\pi}{2}$. Find $k$.

questions.solution:
**It is a quadratic in $\sin\theta$.** Put $s = \sin\theta$:

$2s^{2} - s - 1 = 0$

$(2s + 1)(s - 1) = 0$

$s = -\dfrac12$ or $s = 1$.

**Case 1: $\sin\theta = 1$.**

$\theta = 90°$ — only one solution in the range, since the sine reaches its maximum just once.

**Case 2: $\sin\theta = -\dfrac12$.**

The reference angle is $30°$, and the sine is negative in the **third and fourth** quadrants:

$\theta = 180 + 30 = 210°$

$\theta = 360 - 30 = 330°$

**Solutions: $\mathbf{\theta = 90°, 210°, 330°}$.**

**The method in two steps:** find the **reference angle** from the positive value, then use the quadrant rule (**A**ll, **S**in, **T**an, **C**os) to place every solution in the range.

A calculator alone would have given $-30°$, which is outside the range and only one of the three answers.

**Start with the left-hand side** and use the double angle formulae — always work on one side only, never across the equals sign.

$\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta$, so $1 - \cos 2\theta = 2\sin^{2}\theta$.

(Choosing this form of $\cos 2\theta$ is the key step: it makes the numerator a single term.)

$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

**Substituting:**

$\dfrac{2\sin^{2}\theta}{2\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$ ∎

**Two pieces of advice for identity proofs.**

1. **Start with the more complicated side** — there is more to simplify and fewer choices to make.

2. When $\cos 2\theta$ appears, pick whichever of its three forms produces the function the other side needs. Here we wanted $\sin$, so $1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta$ was the right choice; $2\cos^{2}\theta - 1$ would have gone nowhere.

**A caution:** the identity fails where $\sin 2\theta = 0$, since the left side is then undefined while $\tan\theta$ may not be.

questions.q: Express $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ in the form $R\sin(\theta + \alpha)$, and hence find the maximum value and the value of $\theta$ at which it occurs.
questions.solution:
**Expand the target form:**

$R\sin(\theta + \alpha) = R\sin\theta\cos\alpha + R\cos\theta\sin\alpha$

**Compare coefficients:**

$R\cos\alpha = 3$ and $R\sin\alpha = 4$

**Find $R$** by squaring and adding — the $\sin^{2} + \cos^{2} = 1$ identity does the work:

$R^{2} = 9 + 16 = 25 \Rightarrow R = 5$

**Find $\alpha$** by dividing:

$\tan\alpha = \dfrac43 \Rightarrow \alpha = 0.927$ rad $(53.1°)$

$\mathbf{3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = 5\sin(\theta + 0.927)}$

**Maximum value.** A sine never exceeds 1, so the maximum is $\mathbf{5}$.

It occurs when $\sin(\theta + 0.927) = 1$, that is $\theta + 0.927 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$\theta = 1.571 - 0.927 = \mathbf{0.644}$ rad $(36.9°)$.

**Why this form is so useful.** $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ has no obvious maximum; $5\sin(\theta + 0.927)$ has an obvious one. Two waves of the same frequency always add to a single wave, of amplitude $\sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}}$ — **not** $3 + 4$, because they never peak together.

It also turns an equation such as $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = 2$ into one that can actually be solved.

questions.q: Describe the graph of $y = 2\sin\left(3x\right) + 1$, giving its amplitude, period, maximum and minimum.
questions.solution:
**Start from $y = \sin x$** and apply each change.

**Amplitude 2** — the factor outside stretches it vertically, so it swings $2$ either side of its centre line.

**Period $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$** — the $3$ inside squashes it horizontally, fitting three complete cycles into the usual $2\pi$.

**Translated 1 up** — the centre line is $y = 1$, not $y = 0$.

**Maximum:** $2(1) + 1 = \mathbf{3}$, first at $3x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, i.e. $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

**Minimum:** $2(-1) + 1 = \mathbf{-1}$, at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

**Range:** $-1 \le y \le 3$.

**The general form $y = a\sin(bx + c) + d$:**

• $a$ — amplitude

• $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ — period

• $d$ — vertical shift, the centre line

• $-\dfrac{c}{b}$ — horizontal shift

**Note the asymmetry:** the number **outside** ($a$) multiplies the amplitude directly, but the number **inside** ($b$) **divides** the period. Anything inside the bracket works in reverse.

questions.q: Given that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\theta$ is acute, find $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\sin 2\theta$ without a calculator.
questions.solution:
**Draw the triangle.** $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac34$, so take opposite $= 3$ and adjacent $= 4$.

**Hypotenuse:** $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$.

**Read off the ratios:**

$\sin\theta = \mathbf{\dfrac35}$, $\quad \cos\theta = \mathbf{\dfrac45}$

Both positive, since $\theta$ is acute.

**Double angle:**

$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2 \times \dfrac35 \times \dfrac45 = \mathbf{\dfrac{24}{25}}$

**And for completeness:**

$\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta = 1 - \dfrac{18}{25} = \dfrac{7}{25}$

**Check:** $\left(\dfrac{24}{25}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{7}{25}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{576 + 49}{625} = 1$ ✓

**The triangle is the fastest route** to every other ratio once one is known — far quicker than working through the identities, and it keeps the answers exact.

**If $\theta$ were not acute**, the magnitudes would be the same but the signs would follow the quadrant, so the range of $\theta$ must always be checked.
